sections.h: "The souls of the righteous are in God's hand" (Wisdom 1-5)
sections.b: Wisdom's first chapters are the Bible's richest passage on the soul outside the 66 books. Wisdom will not live in "a soul that schemes evil" (Wisdom 1:4); a lying mouth "kills the soul" (Wisdom 1:11). The ungodly think the mind is a spark that goes out and the breath scatters like air (Wisdom 2:2-3). The book answers that God created the human being "for incorruption" as "an image of his own eternity" (Wisdom 2:23), and that "the souls of the righteous are in God's hand, and no torment will touch them at all" (Wisdom 3:1). To fools they seemed to die, "Yet they are in peace" (Wisdom 3:3), and "their hope is full of immortality" (Wisdom 3:4). Wisdom never says the soul is immortal of itself: "righteousness is immortal" (Wisdom 1:15), and the life of the righteous is held by God. That is why both sides of the later debate, natural immortality and immortality as gift, read this chapter as theirs.

common: Wisdom 3:1-9 is read at funerals in the Catholic Church and at saints' Vespers in the Orthodox churches.

claude.title: Claude's theory: immortality as a relationship
claude.body: Wisdom's own wording points to a middle position that both camps tend to miss. It never calls the soul immortal, but it calls righteousness immortal (1:15), virtue's memory immortality (4:1), and says the righteous live forever because "their reward is in the Lord's keeping" (5:15). Immortality in this book is a relationship kept by God, not a property of the soul. That fits the old man in Justin's Dialogue (the soul lives "since God wills it to live") as well as Wisdom 3:1, and it leaves room for the resurrection hope of the New Testament.

sections.b: The book opens by calling rulers to seek the Lord, because wisdom "will not come into a soul that schemes evil" (Wisdom 1:4). Here wisdom is close to a person: "Wisdom is a spirit that loves people" (Wisdom 1:6), linked with "the holy spirit of discipline" and "the Spirit of the Lord" that fills the world (Wisdom 1:5-7). Despising "wisdom and discipline" is the root of the ungodly's ruin (Wisdom 3:11). The full portrait of Wisdom as a person comes in chapters 7-10.

Wisdom says God made all things for life, "Hades has no royal throne on the earth" (Wisdom 1:14), and "God created the human being for incorruption" (Wisdom 2:23). "But death came into the world through the devil's envy, and those who take his side find out what it is" (Wisdom 2:24). This is one of the earliest texts to link the devil with the death of Genesis 3, and it stands behind 1 Clement's "envy, by which death itself entered into the world." It matches Paul's "death through sin" (Romans 5:12), though Wisdom stresses the death the ungodly choose rather than a death passed to all.

Wisdom uses diabolos once, for the one by whose envy death entered the world (Wisdom 2:24). Set beside Genesis 3, it makes the serpent of Eden the devil, envious of humans made in God's image. 1 Clement joins the verse to the story of Cain and Abel, where the first killing comes from envy (Genesis 4:8). Revelation names "the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9).

Wisdom tells the Servant's story without naming Isaiah. The ungodly plot against "the righteous man" with a line from the Greek Isaiah 3:10; he calls himself a pais, "child" or "servant," of the Lord (Wisdom 2:13), the Greek Isaiah's word for the Servant (Isaiah 52:13); they torture him and condemn him to a shameful death (Wisdom 2:19-20). Then he stands boldly before them, and they are "astonished" (Wisdom 5:1-2) with the verb of Isaiah 52:14. Wisdom is thus one of the earliest readings of Isaiah 53 as the story of the persecuted righteous whom God vindicates. Augustine read the passage as a prophecy of Christ's passion.

sections.h: "If the righteous man is God's son" (Wisdom 2:18)
sections.b: The mockery at the cross, "He has put his trust in God, so God should get him free now, if he takes delight in him. After all, he said, 'I am God's Son'" (Matthew 27:43), joins Psalm 22:8 to words very like Wisdom 2:18: the ungodly test the righteous man, saying that if he is God's son, God will rescue him, and condemn him to "a shameful death" (Wisdom 2:20). Augustine quotes Wisdom 2:12-21 as the place where "the passion of Christ is most openly prophesied."

Wisdom follows Isaiah 56:3-5 against the exclusion of Deuteronomy 23:1: the eunuch who has done nothing lawless and plotted no evil will receive "a special grace and a share in the temple of the Lord, all the more to his heart's delight" (Wisdom 3:14), sweeter than children. The verse stands with the blessing of the pure barren woman (Wisdom 3:13) and the saying "It is better to have no children and have virtue" (Wisdom 4:1).

Where the older stories end with God opening a barren womb, Wisdom calls the barren woman who stays undefiled blessed as she is: "She will have fruit at the visitation of souls" (Wisdom 3:13). Virtue without children is better than many children without virtue, because virtue is remembered with God (Wisdom 4:1-2), while the ungodly's many children are rootless plants (Wisdom 4:3-6). The thought builds on Isaiah 54:1 and comes close to Luke 23:29.

"He pleased God, and God loved him. He lived among sinners, and he was carried off" (Wisdom 4:10). Wisdom names no one, but the verbs are those of the Greek Genesis 5:24 about Enoch, and Sirach 44:16 and Hebrews 11:5 use the same; that match is why the passage is read of him. Wisdom makes the man the model of the righteous who die young: snatched away so that evil would not twist his mind (Wisdom 4:11). Rashi later reads Genesis 5:24 in a similar way, following Genesis Rabbah, which also keeps a rabbi who judged Enoch harshly (Genesis Rabbah 25:1).

Between Isaiah 59:17 and Ephesians 6 stands Wisdom 5:17-20. The Lord takes zeal as his panoplia, "full armor" (the word of Ephesians 6:11, 13), puts on righteousness as a breastplate, honest judgment as a helmet, holiness as a shield that no one can beat, and stern anger as a sword, and creation fights at his side. Paul gives similar armor to believers, adding faith as the shield and the word of God as the sword.

Wisdom ends its judgment scene with the Lord arming himself and making "the created world into a weapon": lightning like arrows from the bow of the clouds, hail as from a siege machine, the sea and rivers, and "a wind of power" (Wisdom 5:21-23). The picture prepares for the book's retelling of the Exodus plagues, where creation fights for the righteous (Wisdom 16:17, 24; Wisdom 19:6).

sections.b: Wisdom answers the hard case of the older teaching that the righteous live long (Proverbs 10:27): "a righteous man who dies before his time will be in rest" (Wisdom 4:7). True old age is understanding and a spotless life (Wisdom 4:8-9), and "The righteous man who has died will condemn the ungodly still alive" (Wisdom 4:16). The reward is moved beyond death, as in Isaiah 57:1-2.

Wisdom reads the suffering and death of the righteous as testing and sacrifice: God "proved them like gold in a smelter's fire and took them to himself like a sacrifice burned whole" (Wisdom 3:6). They will shine, judge nations and wear the crown (Wisdom 3:7-8; Wisdom 5:16). The Orthodox read Wisdom 3:1-9 and 5:15-6:3 at Vespers for martyrs such as the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste.

When their sins are counted, the ungodly come trembling, and their own deeds convict them (Wisdom 4:20). The righteous man they killed stands boldly before them; they confess their error too late (Wisdom 5:1-13). "But the righteous live forever" (Wisdom 5:15), and the Lord arms himself against the wicked. The scene stands between Daniel 7 and 12 and the judgment scenes of the Gospels and Revelation.

sections.h: "The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world" (Wisdom 1:5-7)
sections.b: Wisdom speaks of "the holy spirit of discipline" that runs from deceit (Wisdom 1:5), of wisdom as "a spirit that loves people" (Wisdom 1:6), and of "the Spirit of the Lord" that "has filled the world" and holds all things together (Wisdom 1:7). The Douay-Rheims prints "the Holy Spirit of discipline" at Wisdom 1:5, and in the Roman Missal of 1962 Wisdom 1:7 is the entrance chant of Pentecost. The book's fullest words on God's spirit come at 7:22-8:1 and 9:17.
